title: Arctic foxes

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: One spring a few years ago, Canadian biologists began monitoring a female Arctic fox living on Bylot Island in the Arctic Ocean. At first, there was nothing unusual about the animal's behaviour. She found a den and a mate, and together the pair carried out the exhausting task of rearing 11 hungry pups. But as autumn set in, a switch seemed to flip inside her brain — a switch that caused her to do something that for most other animals her size would be a death sentence: she began to wander. The fox moved northward off the island and onto the permanent Arctic ice cap. She remained there for nearly four months, zigzagging hundreds of kilometres over crumbled ice under conditions that included minus 40°C temperatures.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Records of the species’ unusual behaviour date back more than a century. During his attempt to reach the North Pole in 1895, Norwegian explorer Fridtjof Nansen was amazed to encounter fox footprints as he crossed the Arctic ice cap. Some 80 years later, in the 1970s, researchers on the north shore of Alaska released several Arctic foxes fitted with ear tags. While a few animals turned up in traps hundreds, and in some cases, thousands of kilometres away, most were never seen again. Such findings raised many questions. How do these animals — barely larger than domestic cats — navigate in an environment seemingly devoid of sensory clues? What patterns do their movements take? Are these trips one-way journeys or epic migrations? Unfortunately, given the challenges of the Arctic winter, scientists until recently had few opportunities to learn the answers. In one valiant attempt in 1979, biologist Robert Garrott and his team camped on sea ice, and attached radio collars to foxes which they tried to follow by plane. ‘We learned absolutely nothing,’ Garrott recalls. ‘The place is simply too big, and the foxes are too mobile. They just disappeared.’

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Unlike many inhabitants of the Far North, Arctic foxes don’t hibernate, shelter beneath the snow, or migrate south during the cold months. Instead, they remain active, taking the full cruelty of the Arctic winter head on. How they pull off such a feat has long been a mystery. However, thanks to progress in the 21st century in the field of satellite technology, scientists are now able to track Arctic fox movements during the nine months of the year when the foxes are otherwise inaccessible, and gain a rare glimpse into the animals’ unknown world. In the past, researchers had hints that at least some foxes left land during winter. But they weren't sure whether these were temporary trips away from land, or if the ice was like a second home for the foxes. Recent studies suggest the latter. One of the monitored animals in the latest project roamed over nothing but sea ice for more than five months.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Experts are aware that Arctic foxes have superb navigational abilities, even on the ice cap, which not only lacks permanent landmarks but is also in constant motion due to the push and pull of Arctic Ocean currents. Arctic foxes have been tracked travelling over 2,000 kilometres in just three months during winter, before ending up at the site of their former summer dens. ‘It’s not luck,’ says Dominique Berteaux, the biologist who heads the research team on Bylot Island. ‘It's intentional. They know where they are. They have a very good sense of orientation. It's quite extraordinary.’

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not every fox embarks on an epic journey. This became clear last winter when Berteaux's team tracked 29 foxes, the largest survey to date. One headed south to Baffin Island, tracing a 1,600-kilometre loop that extended as far as the Canadian mainland. Another headed 70 kilometres into Bylot Island's mountainous and largely lifeless interior. Others made shorter trips. Almost half never left Bylot Island, and none of the animals engaged in extreme movements like those seen two years earlier. ‘What we're finding is that these very long movements are not typical,’ says Berteaux.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: So what drives some of the animals to travel such distances? Food is one obvious answer. Researchers have long known that Arctic foxes go on expeditions alongside polar bears in order to scavenge leftover seal remains. They also think the foxes may feast on whale or walrus carcasses that become entombed in sea ice. Extreme wandering, meanwhile, might have less to do with what is available on the ice and more to do with what is not available at home — particularly lemmings, rotund Arctic rodents that undergo periodic population crashes. Researchers suspect that sea ice may provide Arctic foxes with a valuable back-up food source during difficult times.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: This prompts another question: will the species survive as global warming reduces the extent of Arctic sea ice? One possibility is that warmer weather will bring more productivity to the region’s ecosystems, making it less important to find food out on the ice. A likely side effect, however, is the range expansion of red foxes: larger rivals that historically were absent from the Far North, but now are increasingly spreading into the Arctic fox's domain. The current view among many experts is that Arctic foxes will survive, but only on remote islands in greatly reduced numbers. Of course, in the absence of ice, their wandering ways would become a thing of the past.
